title: Species presence, not abundance, made 95% of spatial temperature gradients in 75 community networks; per 1 C, exchange of species in time was 16% of that in space (1948-2025)
abstract: Question: community temperature indices (CTI) follow about 12% of their own spatial temperature slope in time. Does the gap come from membership (which taxa are present: colonisation and local extinction) or from dominance (abundance of resident taxa)? Data: 73 BioTIME 2.0 studies, the North American Breeding Bird Survey and the UK Butterfly Monitoring Scheme; 75 networks, 8,529 grid-box sites, 183,626 site-years, 1948-2025; GHCN_CAMS and HadISST temperature. Method: cross-fitted species temperature indices; an exact split of the abundance-weighted CTI into a membership CTI M and a dominance part D; spatial, slow (trend) and fast (anomaly) slopes; early-half versus late-half gain, loss and reweighting terms with permutation nulls; site-pair spatial benchmarks. The plan was written before outcomes; the window refinements and pair benchmark were added after the first results. Results: the spatial slope was 0.179 C per C, and its dominance share was 0.046 (95% CI 0.015-0.076); in the BBS it was zero. Membership followed 0.125 (0.025-0.285) of its spatial slope; the dominance trend slope was -0.004 (-0.012 to 0.007) and at its null. Membership held 93% of the gap. The planned hypothesis that residents reweight fast but membership lags was not supported. Gained taxa were warm-affinity taxa (+0.055 C per C, z 4.8), but lost taxa were also warm (-0.024); the net exchange was +0.028 (-0.001 to 0.059). Gained taxa had 28% of their count share in abundance in all 72 networks. Per 1 C, temporal exchange was 0.16 (0.01-0.34) of spatial exchange; temporal turnover (0.19) was below spatial turnover at zero distance (0.30) and did not rise with warming. Conclusion: the gap is in warming-driven species exchange, and newcomers stay rare. Limitations: membership change includes detection of rare taxa; STI-linked detection drift is not removed; selectivity in time is uncertain; network-internal STIs.

Early-half versus late-half terms per 1 C of warming after null correction (A), and abundance share against count share of gained and lost taxa (B): newcomers stay rare.
Turnover rate, thermal selectivity and exchange term between site pairs (space) and between half-series (time). Temporal exchange per 1 C is 16% of the spatial value.

citations.reason: We reuse its 75 networks, cross-fitted STI method and build scripts, and divide its CTI gap into membership and dominance parts.
Bird CTI followed less than 10% of warming; our BBS anchor shows that the BBS spatial gradient is all membership.
Spatial CTI slopes hold between nearby routes; we show that these slopes are species-list gradients.
Species-level abundance responses follow 5-14% of gradients in birds; we find that abundance reweighting adds no trend tracking.
Vegetation mediates half of the forested-route gap; we test a general process split across taxa.
Rate-mixture bounds on the 54 network summaries; we use new record-level decompositions instead of the summaries.
Frozen-STI spatial slope is the benchmark for CTI change.
Winter bird turnover without a temperature link; we find weakly thermal background turnover in many networks.
Tree community warming by mortality did not exceed a species-permutation null; our window terms use the same null idea.
Land-cover change did not cause weak bird temperature tracking.
Observer hearing drift is a detection effect that our permutation null cannot remove.
Phenology-detection artefact was too small to explain the gap.
Traffic masking was too small to change the CTI trend.
Insecticide change explained less than 3% of the bird CTI gap.
Bird centroids moved at 14% of the isotherm shift.
Local thermal gradients are real at 5 km resolution.
